3.text: one tale it is related how a wanderer comes to the upper world, where he

4.text: is kindly received, and treated to the best of everything. After a while

5.text: his host offers to get him a bride. The youth assents. His host opens a

6.text: hole in the ground by pulling out the stopper, and the lower world is in full

7.text: view. Five girls are playing ball near a lake. The host angles for one of

8.text: them with a sharp fish-hook. He succeeds in catching her by the navel,

9.text: and drags her up; but he has caught only her “soul,” the body is left down

10.text: below. Her companions wail because of her sudden death. The girl marries

11.text: the youth, and they live for a while with their heavenly host. In the end

12.text: he gives them permission to leave, and he himself lets them down to earth.

13.text: Another way for the dead to ascend to heaven is to follow the smoke

14.text: of their funeral pyre. This is given as a reason for burning dead bodies.

15.text: In one tale a shaman, every time he wishes to visit the upper world, is

16.text: killed and burned on his pyre, and then ascends with the smoke. He comes

17.text: down again in a whirlwind. The reindeer of his sleigh must be caught by the oc-

18.text: cupants of his house as he rushes by: otherwise he will pass by, and never return.

19.text: The Aurora Borealis is chiefly the place of abode for those who die a

20.text: sudden or violent death. The whitish spots are the people who died from

21.text: contagious diseases; the red spots are those stabbed with a knife; the dark

22.text: spots are those strangled by the “spirits” of nervous diseases; the changeable

23.text: rays are deceased people running about and playing ball with a walrus-head

24.text: which is alive. It roars when in motion, after it has been tossed. It wants

25.text: to strike with its tusks anybody who tries to catch it.¹ Men who have been

26.text: strangled with a slip-noose at their own request, have honorary places among

27.text: the spectators; or they themselves may play, but do so in a very awkward

28.text: manner, because of the rope dangling behind them on the ground. According

29.text: to the belief of the Gilyak of the Amur country, the souls of those who die

30.text: a violent death, including suicides, ascend directly to heaven; while those

31.text: who die a natural death remain on earth, or descend underground.²

32.text: One of the sketches (Fig. 235) represents the Aurora Borealis. Two

33.text: cross-lines divide the sky into four equal portions. The centre is the zenith.

34.text: It is surrounded by a circle, which represents its house. The region of

35.text: Dawn is in the left-hand corner, below. In the lower part of the picture

36.text: lies the land of Darkness. The sky is studded with stars. The Aurora

37.text: Borealis is represented by several parallel bands. In the region of the upper-
